answer:
1. The animation shows a grid of squares. Light squares mean the buyer is ahead after ten years, and dark squares mean the renter is ahead. It's built from FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates, and it is labeled "illustrative." Almost all the squares are light, with a thin dark strip in the middle. A caption reads "rent tag 6%: buyer ahead in 92.2%", so under a 6% rent assumption the buyer comes out ahead in 92.2% of the cases.

2. Very little changes across the frames. The grid and the dark strip stay essentially the same. The only changes are the captions. The "rent tag 6%: buyer ahead in 92.2%" line appears in frame 2 and stays through frame 5. The line "the share moves with the rent you assume" appears in frame 5 and stays in frame 6. In frame 6 the first caption is gone.

3. It means that, in this historical data, buying beat renting over a ten-year hold in most of the cases shown, assuming rent at the 6% level. The result depends on the rent assumption, because the share of buyer-ahead cases shifts if you assume different rents. The footer says it is US only, and it is history, not a forecast.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might loosely take away that buying has often come out ahead over ten years, but that the answer depends on the rent figure they use. They would want to test their own local rent assumption.

5. The animation's text suggested the dependence on rent ("the share moves with the rent you assume") and the "history, not a forecast" caveat. It did not suggest buying. The idea that a viewer should test their own rent figure is my own reading of it.
